question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: This year marks a significant moment for the UNESCO IHP as we celebrate the 30th birthday of ecohydrology at UNESCO and 20 years of UNESCO ecohydrology demonstration sites. Today, we reflect back from foundations of the science in Poland to the current global influence of ecohydrology. Ecohydrology rose to answer the fundamental question of how to deal with ecosystem problems in the aquatic environment. As Professor Zalewski, director of the European Regional Centre for Ecohydrology, realized that environmental protection alone is not enough. Hence, by studying the mechanisms that regulate the environmental processes through the interactions between the biota and the water system, ecohydrology was born. With water as a driver for all life, the protection and resilience against challenges in the current climatic context, such as pollution, scarcity, management, and drought, is essential. Thus, the second part of ecohydrology is finding and implementing solutions. From the design of experiments in laboratories to the implementation of real systems, research in ecohydrology looks for nature-based solutions to tackle different problems worldwide. To highlight successful implementations of NBS based on ecohydrological values at the water basin scale, UNESCO has supported the formation of 66 demonstration sites. These span 36 countries across all six continents and are excellent case studies for the ecohydrological approach to water management. This network has developed thanks to the UNESCO demonstration site program that brings together researchers, local governments, and communities from all across the world. Examples include the ecological engineering of Las Dunas in the Cahuayumac microbasin in Peru, the natural migration and remediation of watersheds and lagoon ecosystem in Ghar El Melh, Tunisia, wastewater treatment wetland system in Asmelabad, Pakistan, and the Birmingham urban ecohydrological urban observatory in the Upper Tame catchment in the United Kingdom. Another key development is the international Ecohydrology & Hydrobiology Journal aimed at increasing understanding of water-biota interplay and how this knowledge can be used for decision-making tools. The scope aims to address the priorities of the international initiatives, such as the Millennium Development Goals and the UNESCO IHP. With 26 volumes, the journal incorporates climate change, water quality, pollution, and sustainability, and the latest developments of ecohydrological understanding. The importance of ecohydrology will continue to grow with the need to reduce consumption and alleviate pressure on the environment as climate change will bring about new water challenges. With water being a key element of all aspects of life, these 30 years mark only the beginning. To continue building a resilient future, we look to the youth of today. The Ecohydrology Youth Network brings together young people and aims to support the engagement and the development of ideas within the ecohydrology field. With over 500 members, the network connects young scientists, promotes ecohydrological solutions, and exchanges ideas. The future of ecohydrology is looking bluer and greener. And on that note, happy 30th anniversary of ecohydrology and 20 years of ecohydrology demonstration sites.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Hi, my name is Dr. Gillian Barlow, and I'm here to talk about my poster about antibiotic resistance and the small bowel. Prolonged or repeated use of antibiotics, particularly in early childhood, can negatively impact the gut microbiome and lead to antibiotic resistance. In addition, antibiotic use has been suggested to contribute to the development of small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, or SIBO. However, most of these studies were performed using stool samples. So in this study, we explored the impact of antibiotic use in the small bowel, which is central to nutrient absorption, immune function, and hormone regulation. To do this, we collected duodenal aspirates from subjects undergoing upper endoscopy via our REIMAGINE study and isolated the microbial DNAs and sequenced them. We also plated some of each sample to determine which ones had SIBO, and compared medical histories to see which subjects had used antibiotics in the last six months. In total, 1,052 subjects were analyzed, of whom 214 had taken antibiotics in the last six months. Importantly, we found there was no significant difference in the prevalence of SIBO in subjects who had or had not taken antibiotics. In addition, there were also no differences in duodenal microbiome diversity or richness between the two groups. However, we did find significant differences in antibiotic resistance profiles. Comparing antibiotic resistance ontology, or ARO phenotypes, we found that two were more common in subjects who had taken antibiotics in the last six months. The first was proteins modulating permeability to antibiotics, which confers resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics, that would include penicillins, cephalosporins, and carbapenems. And the second was genes altering cell wall change, which confers resistance to a broad range of antibiotics. Lastly, as far more of the subjects in our antibiotics group were female, we broke the results down by sex. However, we found that there were no differences in the ARO profiles in male versus female subjects. So, what are our take-home messages? Taking antibiotics in the last six months is not associated with an increased prevalence of SIBO, and does not appear to affect microbiome richness or diversity in the small bowel. question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Hi. My name is Ava from the MAST program. And in this study, we're looking at how aging impacts the small intestinal microbiome and its relationship to gastrointestinal symptoms. We know that small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, or SIBO, becomes more common as people get older. But what we're still unclear about is why. Whether it's driven by an increase in total bacterial load or shifts in the microbial composition, or even both. So our aim in this study is to determine if there's a relationship between aging, absolute small bowel microbial loads, microbial community structure, and gastrointestinal symptom severity. To address this, we analyzed duodenal aspirate samples from subjects in the REIMAGINE study. These were patients undergoing upper endoscopy without colon prep. We grouped subjects by age and used metagenomic sequencing to quantify absolute microbial abundance, so not just relative composition, but actual bacterial load. What we found is total bacterial load increases significantly with age, and the prevalence of SIBO rises as well. At the same time, microbial diversity declines in older age groups. When we looked more closely at microbial composition, we found that key Gram-negative bacteria, particularly Escherichia coli and Klebsiella species, increase progressively with age in patients with SIBO. These changes were consistent and significant across all age groups. Then we looked at how this relates to symptoms. In subjects over the age of 50, those with SIBO reported significantly greater symptom severity, including diarrhea, bloating, and abdominal pain. Importantly, these symptoms were strongly associated with the abundance of specific bacterial groups, such as Escherichia and Fusobacterium, rather than bacterial load alone. And also, in older subjects without SIBO, increased bacterial load did not correlate with symptom severity. So simply having more bacteria isn't enough to explain symptoms. It really depends on the microbial composition. So overall, our findings suggest that aging is associated with increased bacterial load and reduced diversity, but symptom severity in older adults is more closely linked to specific microbial signatures rather than total load alone. This highlights the importance of using absolute microbial quantification to better understand, diagnose, and potentially treat SIBO, especially in aging populations. Thank you so much for taking the time to listen to my poster, and be sure to check out the rest of our posters from the MAST program here at DDW. Take care.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: There was a point in time, earlier on in my spiritual awakening journey, when I was concerned with growth and getting better. Not that I don't want to grow now because of course I do, but in the beginning, the pursuit of growth was all-consuming. It was ego-driven. I went to the gym regularly, I meditated, I read self-help, spiritual books, and took notes. I even took up coaching others in an attempt to ditch the nine-to-five scene. None of the habits stuck for more than a few months, but I would always come back to them the following year. Like I said, it was ego-driven. I wanted to do better because, deep down, I felt I wasn't good enough. I felt behind in life, like I should be further along. And although that way of pursuing growth and self-improvement served its purpose, I now understand it's not the best way. Actually, I would even go as far as to say as adding habits to your daily routine for the sole purpose of getting better is the very thing that keeps you from getting better. Often times, our pursuit for better is rooted in social validation. We want to be liked, we want to be accepted, we want to be seen in a particular light. And the problem doesn't come from not being noticed or liked. Often times, along these sorts of external focus journeys, we are seen and liked, but we aren't seen and liked for who we actually are. I believe a better way to improve oneself is not to download a bunch of habits influencers have said that have changed their lives, but to do more of the things you enjoy. Lean into yourself, and forget what the internet says is good or bad. If running is what you love, then run because you love it, not because you think in three months you'll be a different person. If you genuine- if you genuinely enjoy having a couple of beers at the end of the day, have a couple of beers. The biggest lie the self-improvement space sold us was that there's something wrong with who we are, and that we need to fix it. There is nothing wrong with who you are or where you are at in life. We are all walking our own paths, evolving at our own pace. Don't let a stranger on the internet make you feel less than you are. True and lasting change will come when you're ready. And when you're ready, the change will be effortless. Trust your journey. It was carved for you. Thank you for watching. Have a good day.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Good morning, YouTube. Today's journal reading was written on March 17th, 2026, and in this one, I kind of explore ideas of abundance, and I think that's a theme that maybe I've wrestled with a lot throughout my life. Anyway, here it goes. Abundance is found in nothing. Abundance is found in knowing enough. As I write this, I'm sitting back in our brown leather recliner we found sitting outside our dumpster when we first moved here. That probably sounds gross, but it was in good shape, and we needed some furniture. That was roughly six years ago. There was a time in my life where material abundance and worldly status mattered to me. It was something I chased. Where I was, or what I had, was never enough. I needed more. I needed to progress. But then something changed. I don't know when it happened, or why, or what triggered it. All I know is one day, all that once mattered seemed trivial. Among the spiritual community, there's a decent amount of talk about abundance, the law of attraction, and manifestation. If only we align our thoughts and energy with the life and success and the material we desire, all we imagine will be ours. Whether there's any truth to that, that doesn't really matter to me. What does matter to me is why our lives, where we are at this—where—lah, where we are at any given moment is not enough for us. I think we all have ideas in our head of what it means to be abundant and successful, and likely more often than not, those ideas are filled with lavish material items and social recognition from our fellow man. It's what I thought. It's what I chased. But I've come to understand that that's not true abundance. That's not what true success is. True success and abundance is looking around at your life just at it—just as it is right now, and seeing all that you have, all that you've accomplished this far. If you live in America, odds are you have everything you need, plus some. You have a roof over your head, food in the fridge, people who love you. Recognizing the value in all of that you already have is true abundance. Knowing enough in a world that is constantly telling you to go for more, to go for better, is a superpower. It's abundance. Knowing enough is not a lack mindset. It's peaceful sustainability. It's the mindset of the richest people on earth.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Bullet journaling accepts that every day is different rather than trying to impose the same structure each time. This makes it flexible and able to handle whatever comes up. The main point is that bullet journaling embraces chaos with a system that can change as needed. A daily log has not set amount of space, use what you need that day. Some days may take just one page, others more. The monthly log has two pages, one for the calendar and one for tasks. Write events, tasks and notes on the calendar page next to each date. List tasks for the month on the other page. If a task is for a different month, write it in the future log, then add future tasks to the next month's log when that month starts. You can make custom pages for specific topics like health goals or a hobby. Use the index at the front to keep track of all your pages and collections. List the topic and page numbers. Keep adding to the index as needed. This flexible approach accepts that every day is different. The system can grow and change along with your need.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Your bullet journal can be a useful tool for setting and achieving meaningful goals. Start by making a goals collection to write down both big and small goals. This helps transform vague dreams into real objectives. Next, create timelines for your goals, using something like the 5-4-3-2-1 method. Identify goals for the next 5 years, 4 months, 3 weeks, 2 days and 1 hour. You will likely have many goals, so prioritize by carefully considering each one. Ask yourself if the goal is really important and worth the effort. Choose one personal and one professional goal in each timeframe, for a total of 10 priority goals. It's important to regularly re-evaluate your goals to make sure they still matter. One way is with goal sprints, breaking big goals into smaller steps to test your commitment. This can help you focus on goals that inspire you and keep you motivated, long term. Clarification and prioritizing will help make your goals a reality.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: You're not failing when it comes to habits. You're just starting too many at once. Most people don't struggle because they're lazy. They struggle because they try to change their entire life overnight. They want to wake up earlier, start working out, eat healthier, drink more water, meditate, journal, read more, spend less time on their phone, all at the same time. And for a few days, it feels exciting, but then everything falls apart. Not because you're incapable, because your brain can't sustain that much change all at once. If your habits never seem to stick, the problem isn't motivation. It's the way you're trying to build them. Most habits fail because there's no structure behind them. People rely on motivation instead of systems. They tell themselves, "I'll work out after work tomorrow. I'll start eating healthier in a few days. I'll remember to do it." But vague habits don't survive real life because life gets busy, you get tired, your routine changes, your motivation drops, and if there's no repeatable structure, the habit disappears with it. Another mistake people make is setting the barrier too high. They think, "If I'm going to work out, I'm going to do 1 hour. If I'm going to read, I need to read an entire chapter. If I'm going to meal prep, I need to fix my entire diet." Eventually, your brain starts resisting it, not because the goal is bad, because the effort required feels too big to repeat consistently. That's why intensity usually fails. It asks too much before consistency exists. If you want a habit to stick, make it smaller, smaller than you think it should be. Make it so easy your brain has no reason to avoid it. Want to start working out? Don't commit to an hour. Commit to putting your shoes on and doing 5 to 10 minutes. Want to read more? Read one page. Want to meditate? Sit down for 30 seconds. Your goal in the beginning should not be full transformation. It should be repetition because repetition creates familiarity and familiarity lowers resistance. You're not trying to prove how disciplined you are. You should be trying to teach your brain that this is something you do now. Another thing that helps is attaching your habits to something that already exists. Instead of saying, "I'll do it later," anchor it to something specific. After I brush my teeth, I'll stretch. After work, I'll take a walk for 10 minutes. After making my coffee, I'll journal for a few minutes. The less decisions your brain has to make, the easier consistency becomes. That's what systems do. They reduce friction. Here's the part that nobody likes hearing. Consistency is supposed to feel boring sometimes. Social media makes change look exciting and intense, but real progress usually looks repetitive, quiet, simple, unimpressive. A lot of people quit because a habit no longer feels exciting. But habits that last aren't built on excitement. They're built on repeatability. You don't need perfect days. You need enough days repeated over time. Missing one day isn't failure. Starting over every single week is. The goal isn't to become a different person overnight. The goal is to create a system that you can maintain over time. If you want habits that actually stick, stop trying to change everything at once. Make the habit smaller. Remove friction. Repeat it consistently. Build structure around it. Because consistency is not built through intensity. It's built through repetition. Small actions repeated daily will always beat out massive effort that only lasts a week. Until one day, they become automatic. If this helped, subscribe. I'll be breaking down systems for your lifestyle so you can actually build something that works.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: So, we're here at UKREIIF this year, talking all things living UK real estate. The current environment for living real estate in the UK is one with viability challenges and concerns. We've got rising build cost inflation, increased regulation, economic difficulties. What there also is, is a huge amount of opportunity. There is pent-up demand, there is under supply, there is no shortage of debt available, there is capital being deployed. It is a huge time for opportunity. The smart money is moving primarily into affordable housing, I would say, though how you define that depends on a number of factors, but clearly the biggest risk to any investment strategy is take-up and demand at this moment, and so through various lenses people are trying to make sure that whatever it is that they're investing in or developing is affordable for the end user, so that the project is viable long-term. I think there's quite a lot of opportunity for living product, because there is a fundamental requirement and demand for good quality accommodation across all the living sectors, asset classes. Especially when there is a bit of an affordability gap. So, those that can deliver product that meets that demand are going to be very well placed. 2026, for me, has also been the year of co-living. We're seeing more institutionalisation of co-living, in terms of an accepted asset class for co-investors. So, I think the opportunities at the moment, very much from a housebuilders point of view, are in the land market. Slightly longer-term strategic sites, gray belt, something where you can work with a landowner to really maximize the number of homes on a site, and really go out there and get a planning consent. I believe that the opportunities in the living sector lie in working in partnership, both with local governments, local councils, with developers, with capital, trying to bring everybody together to achieve the ultimate goal of delivering more housing for the country. I think the smart money in living is moving to affordable with a small 'a'. That's how we deal with the viability concerns. That's where some degree of public subsidy can unlock delivery. I also see there's huge opportunities in partnerships becoming platforms, with long-term sustainable partnerships between registered providers, developers and investors to unlock delivery at scale.

answer: For years, FIFA President Gianni Infantino has talked about getting more countries involved at a World Cup. That push finally took shape in January 2017 when football's governing body voted to expand the tournament from 32 to 48 teams. Under the new format, there will be 104 matches at this World Cup. That's 40 more than at Qatar 2022. Those games will be played across 16 host cities in the USA, Mexico, and Canada. That's a huge change from the compact 2022 tournament in Qatar where a fan could realistically attend two or even three matches in a single day. The 48 teams will be split into 12 groups of four. The top two from each group plus the eight best third-placed teams will move into a new 32-team knockout phase. From there, the tournament runs through the round of 32, the round of 16, quarterfinals, semifinals, and then the final. By the time we get to the decider at MetLife Stadium in New York, New Jersey, on July the 19th, the champions will have played eight matches. That's one more than the seven required by Argentina when they won Qatar 2022.

For the first time ever, the tournament will be shared across three countries: the United States, Canada, and Mexico, and matches will be played across 16 cities. The competition is expanding, too. Instead of the traditional eight groups, this year's tournament will feature 12, made up of four teams each. 48 national teams will compete, instead of 32. With more teams in the mix, the road to glory could be tougher to predict. The expansion means a record number of matches. Teams will play 104 matches over 39 days, making it the longest ever World Cup run. With more teams involved, there could be more opportunities for underdogs to make their mark. Among those returning to the World Cup include the Democratic Republic of Congo, Haiti, and Iraq, while four debutants are getting their boots on the pitch for the first time. They are Uzbekistan, Jordan, Curacao, and Cape Verde. But staging the World Cup across three countries brings major logistical challenges. Some teams could end up traveling thousands of kilometers between venues, crossing borders and time zones. FIFA has grouped matches regionally to reduce travel, but long journeys may still be unavoidable for teams that progress deep into the tournament. And depending on where they're playing, the climates could be different, from the high altitude of Mexico City to Miami's heat and humidity. To manage that, FIFA has mandated cooling and hydration breaks during matches. Next, technology will play a bigger role than ever before. Every player will have a digital avatar to remodel on-pitch actions. These changes make it easier for officials to see what would go on during fast or obstructed plays, so they can provide more accurate calls for offsides or potential handballs. And then, of course, there are the stars. This could be the last dance for several legends. Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo has confirmed this will be his last World Cup. Argentina's Lionel Messi and Croatia's Luka Modrić are also widely expected to be making their final appearances on the game's biggest stage. For football's greats, one final bow. For a new generation, a chance to make history. The road to World Cup glory is about to begin.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Hi, I'm Dr. Kevin Baum and I lead the research group for Responsible AI and Machine Ethics at the German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence. Being a philosopher and computer scientist, I work on a problem that sounds simple, but that might be one of the most important ones in our lifetimes. The alignment problem. Put simply, it is about getting AI to do what we want in ways we find acceptable. But that framing actually hides the hard part. We live in a pluralist society and we do not agree on what we want or on what counts as acceptable. So aligning AI with human values is more than a technical challenge, it's a sociotechnical one under deep normative uncertainty. At bottom of it, it's a political problem. Whose values, decided by whom, and why? My group works on that challenge from a philosophical and a computer science point of view. We build architectures that make AI reason explicitly about norms and values, resulting in normatively competent systems that can act for the right reasons, state those reasons, and let human challenge and refine them, and we ground all that in philosophical theory. Here's why it matters. AI systems are becoming agents, making decisions in hospitals, courtrooms, and classrooms. The answer is not smarter machines, it is normatively more competent ones. Doing the right things for the right reasons, guided by real humans and keeping responsibility where it belongs.

I've been playing football at a high level for years, training harder than everybody else, taking it more seriously than ever before. The toughest battles in life are given to the strongest warriors, not because life is cruel but because life is precise. You're going to be playing your best football, your confidence is going to be untouchable, the doors are going to start opening up. And that moment right there, that moment is only beautiful because of everything that came before it. The goal in football or in life is not to avoid the hard season. So, if you're in it right now, keep training, keep building, keep showing up every single day for your standards when everything around you feels like it's not. question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: In today's video, I'm going to teach you how to create a line of credit account in QuickBooks Online. Having a line of credit account set up in QuickBooks is essential for tracking borrowed funds and repayments accurately within your financial records. Whether you're managing a small business or keeping personal finances in order, this process will help you stay organized and ensure your books are complete and up to date. If you don't already have a QuickBooks Online account, you can use the link in the description to sign up and get started. Now, let's dive into the steps. First, start by logging into your QuickBooks Online account and navigating to your dashboard. Look to the top right corner of the screen where you'll see a small gear icon. This is your settings menu. Go ahead and click on it to open the options. From the dropdown menu that appears, you'll need to scroll down and select the option labeled "Chart of accounts." This is where all your accounts are managed and organized within QuickBooks. Once you're on the chart of accounts page, look towards the upper right corner of the screen again and click the button labeled "New." This will allow you to create a new account. Next, you'll need to enter a name for the account you're setting up. You can choose something straightforward like "Line of Credit," or use a name that better suits your specific needs. It's helpful to pick a name that makes the account easily recognizable when you're reviewing your records later. After naming the account, it's time to assign the correct account type. In the dropdown menu for account type, select "Long-term Liabilities." This category is appropriate because a line of credit typically represents a financial obligation that spans longer than a year. Once you've set the account type, move to the detail type field. From this list, choose "Notes Payable." This detail type is the most accurate for a line of credit, as it represents loans or borrowings that need to be repaid. question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: We ask it out of habit every single day, but we rarely listen for the truth. "How are you? Are you okay?" "Yeah, I'm fine." It's the ultimate American defense mechanism. We live in a culture that glorifies the grind, praises independence, and tells us to "fake it till we make it." So when things get heavy, our language shrinks. We reduce an entire ocean of burnout, anxiety, and quiet exhaustion into a single automatic wall. "Have you been crying?" "No, just tired." "Just tired." It's the perfect cover-up. Because nobody questions it. In a world where everyone is exhausted, it's easy to hide. But there's a massive difference between needing sleep and being tired of waking up feeling empty. Depression doesn't always look like tears or dramatic breakdowns. In reality, it looks like complete isolation. It's sitting in a crowded room in New York or a quiet suburb in Ohio, surrounded by people, yet feeling entirely invisible. It's building walls so high that even the people who love you can't reach you. "Do you want to talk about it? You can tell me anything." "No, there's nothing to talk about." When someone pushes you away, it's rarely a rejection. Most of the time, they literally just don't have the words. How do you explain a profound sadness that has no specific cause? How do you tell your family or your friends that your life looks great on paper, but feels completely hollow inside? So they say "No," hoping you'll leave them alone, but secretly praying that you won't. They don't need a lecture, they don't need a motivational speech, toxic positivity, or a 10-step plan on how to fix their life. "Do you want a hug?" "Yeah." Sometimes saving a life doesn't take a hero, it doesn't take the perfect words. It just takes the willingness to sit in the dark with someone. The most powerful thing you can say to someone who is drowning isn't "I understand." It's simply, "I'm here, and you don't have to carry this alone." Right now, millions of people are fighting battles they don't talk about. And ironically, the people who spend all their energy checking on everyone else are often the ones drowning the fastest. Do me a favor today. Don't just send a casual text asking "How's it going?" Call someone, look them in the eyes, break through the automatic answers. Because you never truly know how heavy a burden is until you offer to help hold it. Check on your people today.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: The perfect 60-second startup pitch. Imagine you step into an elevator with your dream investor. You have exactly 60 seconds before the doors open. Would you know what to say? Most founders make one big mistake. They try to explain everything about their business. The truth is, your goal isn't to close the investment in 60 seconds. It's to make the investor want another conversation. Here's a simple framework that works. First, start with the problem. What pain are you solving? Keep it simple and relatable. If the investor doesn't understand the problem, they won't care about the solution. Next, explain your solution. In one sentence, describe what your company does. Avoid technical jargon or long explanations. If someone outside your industry can't understand it, it's probably too complicated. Then, explain why now. Why is this the right time for your business? Maybe a new technology has made your solution possible. Maybe customer behavior has changed. Maybe the market is growing rapidly. Investors want to know why this opportunity exists today, not 5 years ago. After that, share your traction. You don't need millions in revenue, but you do need evidence that you're making progress. That could be paying customers, user growth, partnerships, pilot programs, or even a growing waitlist. Traction reduces uncertainty and builds confidence. Finally, finish with the opportunity. Don't end by asking for money. Instead, leave the investor wanting to learn more. Give them a reason to schedule a second meeting. Remember, a great pitch doesn't answer every question. It answers just enough to create curiosity. If an investor walks away wanting to know more, you've done your job. The best founders don't overwhelm investors with information. They tell a clear story, communicate confidence, and make their business easy to understand. Because at the end of the day, investors don't invest in the longest pitch, they invest in the clearest one. If you found this video helpful, subscribe to the Pitch Network for more practical advice on fundraising, networking, and building startups that investors want to back.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: How angel investors actually decide to invest. Imagine you've spent months, maybe even years, building your startup. You finally get a meeting with an angel investor. You walk in, deliver what you think is the perfect pitch, and they pass. So what happened? The truth is, angel investors aren't just investing in ideas. They're investing in founders. They're investing in execution. And most importantly, they're investing in the probability that your business can succeed. Here are the five things they're really looking for. First, the founder. This is by far the most important factor. Investors know that startups rarely go exactly according to plan. Markets change, products evolve, and unexpected problems come up all the time. They're asking themselves one simple question: Can this founder figure it out? A great founder is resilient, adaptable, and able to execute even when things don't go as planned. Second, the problem. Is it a real problem that people genuinely want solved? Or is it just a nice idea? The bigger and more painful the problem, the more valuable the solution becomes. Great businesses solve expensive problems, not minor inconveniences. Third, the market. Even an incredible product has limited potential if it's built for a tiny audience. Investors look for large growing markets because they want companies that can scale. If the opportunity isn't big enough, neither is the return. Fourth, traction. One of the biggest myths is that you need massive revenue before investors will take you seriously. That's simply not true. What investors really want is evidence that people care. That could be growing users, paying customers, partnerships, a waiting list, or strong engagement. Any sign that the market is responding positively reduces the risk of investing. And finally, why you? What's stopping another company from copying your idea tomorrow? Maybe it's your experience, maybe it's your technology, your network, your community, or simply your ability to execute faster than everyone else. The strongest startups don't just have a great idea. They have a compelling reason why they're the best team to bring that idea to life. At the end of the day, angel investing is all about reducing risk. question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Welcome. Today we're exploring how conferences and festivals can minimize technology turnover, reducing costs, extending equipment life, and supporting sustainability across every stage of event design and production. Today's events rely heavily on technology, from digital signage to mobile apps to interactive displays, all designed to elevate audience engagement. But rapid upgrading cycles push many devices out of service long before the end of their usable life. This constant replacement adds financial pressure, creating higher purchasing, storage, and transport costs. With smarter planning, events can maintain quality while utilizing existing equipment more efficiently and sustainably. Tech turnover often stems from a desire to impress with the newest gear, even when older equipment is still functional. This perception-driven cycle leads to high volumes of discarded tablets, displays, LED panels, and networking devices. Replacing equipment too frequently strains event budgets and contributes to growing e-waste streams. Each discarded device contains materials that require proper disposal through licensed recyclers to avoid environmental harm. Strong inventory management helps reduce unnecessary replacements. By keeping accurate records of equipment age, usage, and condition, event teams can clearly determine when upgrades are truly needed. Asset management systems allow devices to be rotated across multiple events, extending their lifespan. These tools also reveal when a piece of equipment can be repaired or refurbished instead of being replaced outright. With better visibility, purchasing decisions become smarter, more cost-effective, and more sustainable. Modular equipment is one of the most valuable strategies for reducing turnover. Interchangeable components allow lighting, audio boards, and AV systems to be repaired easily without replacing entire devices. Firmware upgrades can also extend the useful life of older equipment. Interoperability ensures older and newer devices function together, preventing unnecessary full system upgrades. Planning for modularity reduces both long-term costs and the environmental footprint of constant tech replacement. Not every event requires brand-new technology. Many attendees care far more about meaningful content and clear audiovisual output than the generation of the device being used.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: In 1971, Richard Nixon signed the National Cancer Act and declared war on cancer. The language was deliberate: a war with a target date, the way you'd talk about landing on the moon. 55 years later, cancer still kills about 10 million people a year worldwide. We didn't lose that war through lack of funding. The United States alone has poured well over $100 billion into cancer research since that signature. We lost it because the enemy was never a single enemy. That's the part the fundraising campaigns skip. Cancer isn't a disease. It's a category closer to infection than flu. Breast cancer alone splits into at least four molecularly distinct diseases that happen to grow in the same organ. Lung cancer, pancreatic cancer, leukemia: different biology, different mutations, different behavior, filed under one word because they share a symptom: cells that won't stop dividing. Asking for a cure for cancer is a little like asking for a cure for infection. Which infection? Which mechanism? Which host? Point one: The enemy evolves faster than you can aim. Here's the detail oncologists live with and rarely get to explain on camera: a tumor isn't one clone of identical cells. Peter Nowell described this back in 1976 in a paper called "The Clonal Evolution of Tumor Cell Populations," and the idea has only gotten scarier with better sequencing. A single tumor is a population: genetically diverse, competing internally, mutating with every division. Give it a drug, and you're not killing the tumor. You're running a selection experiment. The cells sensitive to the drug die. The handful that happened to carry a resistance mutation before treatment even started now have the whole tumor to themselves, no competition left. Six months later, the cancer comes back, and it comes back immune to the exact drug that shrank it. This is why remission and cure are different words. Oncologists know the difference intimately.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: I am presenting our work, towards calibrating prompt tuning of vision-language models. This work focuses on improving the reliability of prompt-tuned CLIP models. Our main goal is not only to improve accuracy, but also to make the model's confidence more trustworthy. Prompt tuning is widely used because it adapts CLIP efficiently without updating the full model. However, most existing methods mainly focus on classification accuracy. In real-world applications, accuracy alone is not enough. A model must also know how confident it should be. If a model gives high confidence to wrong predictions, it becomes risky in areas such as medical imaging, autonomous systems, and safety-critical AI. Therefore, models' predicted confidence should equal to the true likelihood or model predicted accuracy. This will ensure that the model's predicted confidence is calibrated. Post-hoc calibration can adjust confidence after training, but it cannot prevent embedding drift caused during prompt tuning. Our key observation is that prompt tuning creates a dual miscalibration problem. For base classes, the model often becomes underconfident because the logit margins are reduced. For novel classes, the model becomes overconfident because the margins become inflated or unstable. The reliability diagrams and margin analysis show that margin behavior affects base and novel classes differently. Therefore, we need a train-time method that controls both logit margins and text embedding geometry, which preserves CLIP geometry by preventing prompt-induced semantic drift and stabilizes class relations, reducing overconfident wrong predictions, thereby lowering calibration error. To solve this, we propose two complementary losses. First, the mean variance margin loss stabilizes the logit gap between the ground-truth class and the strongest incorrect class. This helps improve confidence separation. Second, the text moment matching loss preserves CLIP's original text embedding geometry by matching the distribution of tuned text embeddings with frozen CLIP embeddings. The total loss combines cross-entropy, margin regularization, and moment matching. Together, they reduce base class underconfidence and novel class overconfidence. Margin loss alone is useful, but it can still create high-confidence wrong predictions, especially on novel classes. This happens because if the model predicts the wrong class, increasing the margin can make that wrong prediction even more confident. Moment matching solves this by preserving semantic geometry. So, margin improves discriminability, while moment matching prevents semantic drift. Their combination gives better calibration, especially for novel classes. We evaluate the method on 11 datasets: ImageNet, Caltech-101, Pets, Cars, Flowers...

If you handed me the keys tomorrow and said 'Go back,' I'd burn them.
But listen,
there's a part of me that still walks those three meters by two and a half,
that still feels the quiet drop when the unit locks down.

Picture it.
Green door, heavy bolt,
grey vinyl-covered cabin wood,
tiny desk, bench that bites your spine, bed thinner than regret, toilet right there, no hiding.
Sink, small curtain with its ten-centimeter rule so they can always see you breathing.
Church guitar leaning against the wall like it's waiting for permission to sing, that's it.
That's the whole kingdom. And yet, when the day died and the televisions faded to mumbles, some footsteps echoed and then stopped, that box became still.
No notifications,
no opinions screaming from screens, 
no endless choices pretending to be freedom,
just me
and my mind.
They controlled everything else.

Time,
light,
movement,
who I spoke to,
when I ate,
when I pissed. Razor wire outside, laughing at the sky. But the mind, they couldn't touch it.
In that cage, my thoughts got room to stretch, to roam, to question everything I ever preached from a pulpit, to sit with doubt instead of burying it under sermons. Meditation wasn't an effort, it just happened like breathing,
like the fan humming, low light when the heat creeping through the pipe, a summer sweat turning the air to soup. I'd joke with the boys heading back to my chalet, make them laugh, 'it's a bloody cell, Malcolm.' Yeah, I'd say.
But tonight, it's my university.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Have you ever been lying awake at 2:00 a.m. feeling a physical weight in your chest while your mind races through a tornado of unfinished tasks, looming deadlines and vague anxieties? That sensation signals a specific biological chain reaction taking place in your nervous system. When you perceive a threat, even something as small as a tense email, your brain's threat detection center, the amygdala, fires an alarm and floods your system with cortisol. If this stress stays chronic, neuroimaging shows that your amygdala actually grows larger and more reactive, while your prefrontal cortex, the area responsible for rational executive planning, shrinks and effectively goes offline. To break this cycle, you need a mechanism called cognitive diffusion. By taking those chaotic, swirling thoughts out of your head and translating them into physical words on a page, you force your rational prefrontal cortex to re-engage, which physically turns down the amygdala's alarm system. The worry dump is a structured, analog practice designed to create this distance. It requires putting pen to paper to begin the process of externalization. Grab a physical pen, a piece of paper, and a timer. We are going to walk through this exact process together right now. Moving thoughts onto paper provides a physiological intervention to stall cortisol and reclaim your cognitive control. Step one is to find a quiet, private space where you will not be interrupted. You need an environment where your analytical left brain can focus on the physical act of writing, giving your creative right brain the safety to wander and release everything it's holding onto. Set your timer for exactly five minutes. When it starts, your only job is to write down every single worry, task, and anxious thought currently occupying your mind. Here is the single most critical rule for this phase: you must write continuously. Do not pause to organize your thoughts. Do not prioritize the list. And do not stop to analyze why you are stressed about a certain item. Ignore your inner critic. If you stop to correct your spelling or fix your grammar, you will pull yourself out of the flow and stall the exercise. Keep your pen moving. If your mind suddenly goes blank and you run out of things to say, simply rewrite your last sentence over and over again until a new thought emerges, or until the timer officially sounds. Your output does not need to make sense to anyone else. A single word, a fragmented phrase, or a complete sentence are all equally valid forms of output. Just get it on the page.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer:
Have you ever written something in your journal, re-read it, and thought, "that sounds absolutely nothing like me"?
Here's a thing that doesn't get talked about enough: most people's journal entries sound like they're being written for an audience. Not a real audience—an imaginary one. Some future version of themselves who's going to judge the quality of the writing. Or worse, some hypothetical person who might one day read it. And so, instead of writing, "I'm absolutely furious, and I don't even fully understand why," you write, "today was challenging, and I'm processing some complex emotions." And then you close the journal feeling like you just filed a report rather than said anything true. This is the invisible reader problem, and it's the actual reason most people find journaling uncomfortable. Not because they're bad at it, but because they're performing instead of writing. So why does this happen? Because we've been trained our whole lives to write for a reader: school essays, work emails, texts to people we want to impress. Everything we write has an audience in mind, and we've calibrated our language to manage how that audience sees us. A journal asks you to do the opposite: write for no one. And that turns out to be genuinely hard, especially at first, because your brain keeps switching into "how does this sound?" mode rather than "what is actually true?" mode. The result is entries that are technically accurate but emotionally hollow. The words are right, but the voice isn't yours, and you can feel it when you re-read it—that slight uncanny valley feeling where you recognize the handwriting, but not the person. Honest journaling sounds a lot like how you'd tell a story to your best friend at midnight: short sentences, incomplete thoughts, words you'd never use in formal writing, repetition, contradiction, starting a sentence and stopping halfway through because you realized something while you were writing it. It doesn't have to be coherent. It doesn't have to conclude anything. It doesn't have to read well. The only job it has to do is be true.

Most people assume that putting pain into words works because it lets something out, but release was never really the point. What actually changes you on the page looks more like construction than release, and it explains why some people write for years and feel exactly the same, while others rewire their relationship to a single memory in four short sessions. In the 1980s, the psychologist James Pennebaker ran an experiment that seemed almost too simple to matter. He asked people to write about their most upsetting, unresolved experiences for 15 to 20 minutes, four days in a row. No structure, no therapist, no feedback, just a blank page and permission to be honest. Some of the people in that study wrote about things they had never told another living person. Health visits dropped in the months that followed. Immune markers improved. People slept better and reported less physical pain, and none of it involved anyone hearing their story out loud. Here is where it gets stranger. Pennebaker and later researchers went back through the writing itself, word by word, looking for what separated the people who improved from the people who didn't. It wasn't how much emotion they expressed. It wasn't how many painful details they included. It was whether their language changed. The people who benefited most were the ones whose sentences shifted across those four days from chaos toward explanation. They started using more words like because, realize, and understand. Their writing stopped being a wound repeated on the page and became something closer to a story with a cause and an effect. That shift has a name in psychology: insight. And it turns out insight, not catharsis, is what your mind is actually rewarded for.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Hello and welcome to This Week in Review. This is our weekly segment that's designed to highlight a few important developments that you might have missed this week, and we'll talk about what they mean for markets, and, most importantly, the potential impact for investors. To stay up to date with our latest market insights, subscribe to our YouTube channel or visit fisherinvestments.com. Now, let's review what happened this week. First, the Fed meeting. On Wednesday, the Federal Open Market Committee, or FOMC, voted to hold the interest rate steady at 3.5 to 3.75%. This was the fifth straight meeting without an interest rate change. It was also a split decision, and three members voted to hike rates by 25 basis points. Headlines quickly seized on the story of a divided Fed, but we wouldn't really read too much into that. Differing opinions among Fed officials tells us very little about what the committee will do next, and dissenting votes don't make a rate hike more or less likely in the meetings ahead. Some investors may also worry that Chairman Kevin Warsh's decision to step back from so-called forward guidance may make monetary policy harder to predict or less transparent. We see that differently. Central banks can, and often do, change their minds without notice based on changing economic data or fundamentals. So rather than trying to guess their next move, we think investors are better served by keeping their focus on the broader fundamentals driving markets. Central bank decisions are just one of many forces shaping the global economy and capital markets, and while we believe a rate hike would be a mistake, the talk today is of small hikes. And, really importantly, even a hike or two from here would leave policy rates within a range that this bull market has already successfully navigated. Additionally, when we look around the developed world, yield curves remain steep and healthy. For long-term investors, that's perspective worth holding on to.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Clorox is a good example of a defensive consumer staples business that the market once priced for certainty, then sharply repriced when that certainty broke down. In the pandemic era, investors were willing to pay a premium for bleach, disinfecting and household staples because demand looked unusually strong and durable. In hindsight, that was one of the market's big mistakes. It capitalized peak demand as if it were normal demand. Then the opposite happened. The August 2023 cyberattack followed by ERP-related shipment disruption in fiscal 2024 reminded investors that even a boring staples company can suffer real operational volatility. But Clorox also had real successes. Fiscal 2024 gross margin rose to 43.8%, adjusted EPS reached $6.10, and operating cash flow climbed to $1.04 billion as cost savings and recovery actions took hold. Today the stock looks much less loved. Clorox is trading around $132.85 with a trailing PE of about 21.8x. Against management's fiscal 2025 adjusted EPS outlook of $6.55 to $6.80, the stock is trading at roughly 19 to 20x forward earnings. The quarterly dividend is $1.22 or $4.88 annualized, which puts the yield near 3.7% at the current price. For a company that historically often attracted a much richer multiple because of brand strength, resilience and dividend dependability, that is a meaningful derating. The market is no longer paying up for Clorox as a premium safe haven. It is pricing it more like a mature business that has to prove earnings quality again. The reason the multiple is compressed is not that the brands stopped mattering. It is that fiscal 2025 is messy. In Q1 FY25, net sales fell 15% to $1.39 billion, organic sales were down 15%, and gross margin slipped to 38.8% from 42.1%. Management kept full-year guidance, but said results were likely to land toward the lower end because earlier order fulfillment problems caused consumption and market share losses.

Today on Forbes, the highest paid podcasters of 2026.

When Jay Shetty started his podcast, On Purpose, in 2019, he remembers people telling him he was too late. The medium was already saturated, they said, with little room for growth. And wasn't he really just a content creator?

Seven years later, the 38-year-old self-help guru hosts one of the most popular podcasts in the world, competing not only with the biggest TV, radio, and internet-native talk shows, but blurring the lines between them entirely. Just as many people watch his lengthy interviews with celebrities, including Michelle Obama and Matt Damon, on YouTube, as listen on the iHeartMedia Network. Distribution deals that Forbes estimates paid Shetty $21 million over the past 12 months.

And when those deals expired this year, Shetty landed a new kind of contract, in which the audio and video of his show will not only be distributed by Spotify, it will also stream on Netflix, with the two companies combining to pay him an estimated $100 million over the next 3 years. Shetty tells Forbes, quote, "When I started, video wasn't normal for a podcast. Now we have the four largest streamers bidding for the show. To see that kind of interest and enthusiasm was pretty amazing, for me and for the industry overall."

The impressive thing about mega-deals like Shetty's is that, unlike the makers of movies, TV, or other forms of entertainment, podcasters retain ownership of their shows' underlying IP, meaning networks and platforms are paying millions just to license it as a distributor and ad sales partner for a set number of years. That's one reason why premium streaming giants like Netflix, Hulu, and Tubi had largely ignored the industry's rise over the past decade, allowing YouTube to grow into the largest podcasting platform in the world.

But beginning in 2025, hoping to cut into YouTube's dominance over engagement time, the streamers have made a splashy entrance. Industry dealmakers say that after Netflix's initial $1 million to $2 million bids for top podcasts were roundly rejected, the streamer adopted a strategy similar to the one it used previously to capture market share in scripted television: overpaying to lure talent away from incumbent platforms. Offers of $10 million or more per year, on a one- or two-year trial term, eventually convinced marquee shows from Spotify, iHeart, and Barstool Sports to sign on. Goalhanger, a UK-based podcast network, reportedly landed $19 million from Netflix to stream just 40 episodes of its daily talk show, The Rest Is Football, during the World Cup. question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Let's talk about this paper titled Generative Adversarial Perturbation with Cross-Paradigm Transferability on Localized Crowd Counting. We have seen evasion attacks on all kinds of vision tasks, classification, face recognition to name a few, but crowd models are relatively less explored. They are more complex than the classification task, but they inherit the same weakness that other deep vision models suffer. And most importantly, they are widely deployed in real life scenarios such as public safety, retail analytics and so on. So an undercounting attack could be a safety risk. As we can see a clean example on the right, while passed by a model it outputs 428 people and their locations. However, if small adversarial perturbation is added, it slashes this prediction by over 40% and we get 285 people. So, the previous studies on crowd models are mostly patch-based attacks and they are limited to only density map-based models. So naturally, the question emerges is that can adversarial perturbations transfer across heterogeneous localized crowd counting paradigms such as density map and point regression models? So, to accomplish this attack, we design a perturbation generator that takes clean image as input and outputs the perturbation noise, and this noise is added to the clean image to produce the adversarial image. For black-box transferability, we design a loss function keeping the transferability, imperceptibility and effectiveness goal in mind. Our hypothesis is that even though these models vary by outputs, they share similar backbone architecture such as VGG, ResNet and same weights. So, we our, we hypothesis that this drives the transferability. On the other hand, the crowd scenes are low-frequency dominated, so we suppress the high-frequency and magnitude of the noise for, for subtle perturbation. And lastly, the effectiveness between two paradigms of models come from model-specific loss. So, density map models do the density suppression, and point regression-based models perform logit suppression. Together, this combined loss govern the training. So, this is a sample instance of adversarial examples, where adversarial perturbations are added to the clean images for various lighting conditions.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Hi there, I'm David, and in the next few minutes, I present a short summary of our paper VerifySHAP, or VerySHAP for short, on computing provable bounds for the exact Shapley values of neural networks. SHAP is a popular feature importance technique that can help us explain deep neural networks. The goal is, for example, to find out what influence an input feature, such as the arrow in this image, has on the prediction a neural network makes. SHAP provides such importance scores by computing what is called the Shapley value of each input feature. So, for example, for this arrow feature, we look at a combination of the other features, once with the arrow present, here in yellow, and once with the arrow absent, here in pink. We then use a value function V to mask out the missing features and evaluate the network on that new input with the masked-out features. We then subtract the network output we get when the arrow is absent from the output we get when the arrow is present to compute what is called the contribution delta of this arrow feature. However, SHAP does not only look at one such combination of input features, but looks at all of the combinations of the other input features that we can have. This means that computing Shapley values requires enumerating an exponential number of these feature combinations that are also called coalitions. Because this clearly does not scale very well, previous work has investigated different statistical estimators that only sample a certain number of coalitions. While this is a lot more scalable, these techniques don't necessarily tell us how far off they are with an individual estimate, which can be problematic in sensitive applications. Additionally, for empirically evaluating these SHAP estimators, we need to know the ground-truth exact Shapley values. For these reasons, we introduce VerySHAP, a new algorithm for computing the exact Shapley values of neural networks faster on higher-dimensional feature spaces, and computing guaranteed lower and upper bounds on Shapley values using ideas from neural network verification. The key idea from neural network verification that we leverage is bound propagation. Bound propagation allows us to propagate an entire set of input features, such as this entire coalition space, through the contribution function. And then we obtain a guaranteed lower bound and a guaranteed upper bound on the contribution. We can then plug these bounds into the SHAP equation, and obtain a guaranteed lower bound and a guaranteed upper bound on the Shapley value itself.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Hello everyone, I'm Liangcong from KU Leuven. I'm glad to present our work, Neighbor MAE: Exploiting Spatial Dependencies between Neighboring Earth Observation Images in Masked Autoencoder Pre-training. The main idea of this work is simple. In Earth observation, images are not isolated samples. They are observations of the continuous Earth's surface. So instead of training masked autoencoder on each image independently, we ask whether neighboring images can provide useful spatial context for masked autoencoder pre-training. Masked image modeling has become a popular self-supervised learning strategy for Earth observation. The model masks parts of an image and learns to reconstruct the missing region. However, most existing MIM methods reconstruct a single image tile independently. This is a simplification of Earth observation data because satellite and aerial images are naturally spatially connected. Neighboring images often share useful information, such as terrain structure, land use, continuity, roads, buildings, and infrastructure patterns. At the same time, neighboring views may also differ in acquisition time, viewpoints, or sensor conditions. This means neighboring images provide varied signals, shared spatial context, and natural variations. Therefore, we ask: can neighboring images provide useful context for masked image modeling? To answer this question, we propose Neighbor MAE, which extends MAE from single image reconstruction to joint reconstruction of neighboring Earth observation images. The method has five main components. First, neighbor sampling: we use geospatial metadata to sample neighboring Earth observation images based on the intersection over union of the spatial footprints.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Hello, everyone. I'm Jiayin Jin from Hangzhou City University. Today, I'm excited to present our CVPR 2024 paper, UltrasoundCLIP: Semantic-Aware Contrastive Pre-training for Ultrasound Image-Text Understanding. Ultrasound is one of the most widely used imaging modalities in clinical practice. However, ultrasound vision-language learning remains under-explored because of heterogeneous diagnostic attributes and weak image-text alignment. To address this problem, we propose a semantic-aware ultrasound vision-language framework, together with a large-scale ultrasound image-text dataset. Unlike natural images, ultrasound images are highly challenging for vision-language learning. First, ultrasound diagnosis involves heterogeneous diagnostic attributes. For the same lesion, radiologists may describe multiple diagnostic attributes, such as echogenicity, margins, internal characteristics, and calcification. Second, ultrasound images from different organs often look visually similar, even though they correspond to completely different anatomical structures and diagnostic semantics. Because ultrasound image-text pairs often exhibit weak semantic alignment, directly applying conventional CLIP-style contrastive learning is insufficient for ultrasound understanding. This motivates the need for semantic-aware ultrasound representation learning. To address these challenges, we first construct US365K, the first large-scale dedicated ultrasound image-text dataset. The dataset contains over 364,000 image-text pairs collected from more than 11,000 clinical cases, spanning diverse organs and pathological findings. More importantly, we introduce UDT, which stands for Unified Ultrasound Diagnostic Taxonomy. UDT standardizes both anatomical hierarchy and ultrasound diagnostic attributes, providing structured semantic knowledge for ultrasound understanding. This taxonomy serves as the semantic foundation of our framework.

So, basically we first start off with sample collection where we isolate live cancer cells from different tumor types such as biopsy resections, ascites or pleural fluids and blood or bone marrow aspirates. So, we then perform an ex vivo sensitivity test on the isolated cancer cells by treating them with 12 drugs in a mix of combinations based on proprietary design. So, we then measure the cell viability and use it for Opti-My analysis which then generates a final test report that ranks the top single, two, three and four drug combinations including any relevant clinical trial references. question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Zero-shot anomaly detection, which aims to detect anomalies in unseen categories, has recently attracted significant attention. In this work, we propose MOE-CLIP: Patch-Specialized Experts for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection. To perform zero-shot anomaly detection, existing studies primarily use pre-trained CLIP models and apply adapter fine-tuning methods to adapt them to the anomaly detection task. However, conventional approaches process all patches in a monolithic, patch-agnostic manner, without considering the unique characteristics of each patch, such as background patches or anomalous patches. To address this, we propose MOE-CLIP, a mixture-of-experts-based CLIP adaptation method that dynamically selects the most suitable expert for each patch. However, simply applying a mixture-of-experts framework leads to a functional redundancy problem among experts, where multiple experts learn highly similar representations instead of diverse knowledge. Therefore, we further propose FOFS and ETF loss, which encourage each expert to learn distinct and complementary knowledge. Here is the framework of our proposed MOE-CLIP. First, the mixture of LoRA experts module is inserted into the vision encoder layers, enabling dynamic expert selection and adaptation according to the characteristics of each image patch. The approach for achieving expert specialization, FOFS, is a technique applied at the input stage that enforces role separation among experts through the LoRA A matrices. Specifically, it decomposes the input feature space into multiple orthogonal subspaces, forcing each expert to observe only its own unique information without physical overlap with other experts.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Most candidates memorize PE journal entries and still fail the interview. Why? Because the interviewer is not testing debit and credit only. They are testing cash, NAV, investor capital and LP reporting. Take one private equity fund case: commitment $100 million, capital called $20 million, investment made $15 million, fund expense $1 million, management fee $2 million, fair value $18 million, exit $18 million, distribution to LPs $5 million. Here is the scoreboard. After every entry, ask: did cash move? Did NAV move? Capital activity or performance? What reaches LP reporting? First, capital call. The fund calls 20 million from LPs. Debit cash 20 million, credit investor capital 20 million. Cash increases, investor capital increases, but performance has not improved. This is capital activity, not income. Capital call brings cash, it does not create profit. Second, investment made. The fund invests 15 million into a portfolio company or SPV. Debit investment 15 million, credit cash 15 million. Cash goes down, investment asset goes up, but there is no immediate gain. Cash became investment, that is the trap. Investment made is not an expense and it does not automatically increase NAV. Third, fund expense. Assume 1 million of audit, legal or admin expense. Debit fund expense 1 million, credit expense payable or cash 1 million. This hits P&L, so NAV reduces. LP reporting shows fund level expense impact. The trap: fund expense is not capital activity. It reduces NAV because it hits P&L.

question: Transcribe the audio to text

What I did change, I didn't drink extreme amounts of caffeine because before I fell into anxiety DPDR, I would drink like, and I'm saying insane amounts of caffeine, not just, you know, a few cups of coffee. And I only stopped that because it was just generally unhealthy. Outside of that, I didn't change any actual things regarding my personality or regarding my behaviors at large. What I did change, however, is my understanding of anxiety, depersonalization, derealization, and nervous system sensitization. I suffered for two years because I didn't actually understand these concepts wholeheartedly. And a part of me kept wondering, "Maybe it's something worse," and that worry, in and of itself, kept it alive. Once I fully understood these concepts, and how they're intertwined, and how our nervous system operates, and the reason it produces these types of symptoms, I was able to change my relationship with the symptoms, which inevitably reduced the fear of the symptoms, which allowed me to let them exist alongside me while I lived life normally, still doing the, quote unquote, "crappy" things I would do in my behaviors. And despite my nervous system being incredibly sensitized for two years straight, and I mean like, terrible symptoms for two years straight, I actually recovered pretty quickly after I stopped caring about it. The hardest part is just reaching the point where you don't care. And truthfully, that just comes from going into the symptoms, and living life as normally as you possibly can, allowing them to come with you, labeling them as what they are, as just products of sensitization, and allowing them to take their time, take as much time as they need to. answer: I wanted to share a few reflections around this post because I think some of the ideas can be a bit unfamiliar at first, specifically when trying to understand what we mean by these big ambiguous terms: movement, movement practice, or movement-oriented approach. I chose to start with fitness as a reference because it's the main cultural lens that many of us have inherited when thinking about the body or when thinking about physicality. One of the more important distinctions that I wanted to start with is that movement is not something that we can push or force back into fitness. It's actually the other way around: fitness ends up being nestled inside of movement. And this is something that I see regularly when I look out in the world and I see how movement is being represented. It's represented as movements, things that we do that are isolated in skill or meant to represent some particular outcome, yet it's not encapsulating this unique wholeness that movement is meant to offer. It doesn't mean that fitness is wrong when we think about this nestling or this being smaller than movement, it just means that it's incomplete. And like I said, fitness culture tends to narrow the conversation of the body towards isolated outcomes: strength, flexibility, aesthetics, performance, body comp, and so on. None of these are bad and they can all be valuable, but they don't represent the whole picture. And what we're calling the whole picture in this case is movement, this larger perspective, this larger ongoing study. Implicitly, the question fitness often asks is how can I improve the look or performance of the parts? What we're more interested in through a movement lens is how do these parts participate in the use of the whole? This shift in this way of viewing changes everything.

answer: Becky Chambers' A Psalm for the Wild-Built is a thoughtful, calming story that blends hope, philosophy, and adventure into a deeply human journey. Here's a friendly, engaging audiobook summary style script designed for around 10 to 11 minutes of narration. In a world where people often feel exhausted, disconnected, and overwhelmed by the pressure to constantly do more, imagine a future where humanity actually chose a different path. A future where society stepped away from endless consumption and rebuilt itself around balance, sustainability, and peace. Now, imagine that, one day, after centuries of silence, a robot walks out of the wilderness and asks a simple but life-changing question. "What do people need?" That's the heart of A Psalm for the Wild-Built, a beautifully quiet yet powerful novella by Becky Chambers. This isn't a story packed with giant battles or dramatic twists. Instead, it's the kind of story that gently sits beside you and asks you to think about your own life, your purpose, and what truly makes you happy. And by the end, it leaves you feeling strangely comforted, like someone finally gave you permission to breathe. The story takes place on the moon of Panga where humans once lived alongside robots, but long ago, the robots gained self-awareness and decided they no longer wanted to serve humanity. Instead of fighting, the robots peacefully walked away into the wilderness and humans let them go. Over time, people adapted. Society became slower, greener, and more community focused. Technology still exists, but it no longer controls people's lives. The world Becky Chambers creates feels hopeful because it imagines humanity learning from its mistakes instead of repeating them forever. At the center of this story is a character named Sibling Dex, a tea monk. In this world, monks don't simply live in temples. They travel around offering tea and emotional support to anyone who needs comfort. Dex spends their days listening to people's worries, helping them process emotions, and giving them a brief moment of peace in a busy life. On the surface, it sounds meaningful and fulfilling, but despite helping everyone else, Dex feels restless inside. There's an emptiness they can't explain. A quiet voice keeps asking, "Is this really all there is?" That question becomes the emotional engine of the story.

answer: In 2016, Casey Neistat ended the most-watched daily vlog on the internet at the exact moment it was still growing. 5 million subscribers, over a billion views, revenue climbing every month. answer: Maya wrote in a gratitude journal every morning for 19 days. Then three mornings in a row, she didn't. Most habit apps would have shamed her back. Arrive doesn't. question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: The morning after I killed myself, will I still wake to my mother's prayer, her voice trembling softly between incense and faith, as if God still listens to tired women before sunrise? Will I still hear my father's familiar scolding for not waking up early enough, those small ordinary rants I once mistook for irritation, never realizing they were love wearing a rough voice? Will I still receive those annoying texts from my manager, those weekend meetings I hate with all my heart, and still secretly laugh at how life never asks whether we are tired before demanding more? Will my best friend still wait outside her house for me, ready to pull me away from this suffocating city life, just for an hour, just to remind me that breathing is still possible? Will my mother still save strawberries for me because she remembers what I like, even when I forget what it feels like to be loved? Will my father still stand outside the main gate of our house if I come home late from work, pretending he was just walking outside after having dinner, when really he was waiting to make sure I returned safely? Will those annoying relatives still ask those annoying questions about my marriage, my future, my life, as if they know anything about the storms a quiet person survives without making a sound? No. The day after I leave, none of it will reach me. Not the daily noises that make me frustrated every day. Not the love hidden inside that noise. Not my loved ones waiting for me to reach home safely. Not my parents worrying about my safety. Not the ordinary little things that look so small until I imagined a world without them. And maybe that is the tragedy of hopelessness. It does not always come because life has no love in it. Sometimes it comes because pain grows so loud that it drowns out the love that was there all along. While I was losing hope, everyone around me was still quietly holding hope for me.
