question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: You ever notice how some people look completely fine on the outside? But something about them feels tired? Not physically tired. Soul tired. They wake up, go to work, answer texts, laugh at the right moments, pay bills, scroll their phone at night, and repeat the same cycle over and over again like a machine pretending to be a human being. And nobody notices because nothing is technically wrong. That's the terrifying part. Quiet desperation doesn't always look like a breakdown. Sometimes it looks like functioning perfectly while slowly dying inside. Henry David Thoreau once wrote that most men live lives of quiet desperation, and the older I get, the more disturbing that sentence becomes. Because desperation is easy to recognize when it's loud. When someone's screaming, spiraling, crashing out, everybody sees it. But quiet desperation, that hides behind routines, behind careers, behind relationships, behind smiling photos, and "I'm good" responses. It's the kind of suffering that learns how to behave, and I think a lot of people fall into it without even realizing it. It starts with tiny compromises, tiny betrayals of yourself. "I'll chase my dream later." "I'll settle for this job for now." "I'll stay in this relationship because at least it's familiar." And at first, it feels temporary, but temporary has a way of becoming permanent when fear gets comfortable. Years pass. Your responsibilities grow roots around you, and one day you wake up realizing you built an entire life around survival, but forgot to include yourself in it. That's why some people feel empty even after getting everything they thought they wanted. Because achievement without alignment creates exhaustion. You can win the game and still hate waking up in the morning. You can make money and still feel spiritually bankrupt. You can be surrounded by people and still feel emotionally isolated. Quiet desperation is the gap between the life you're living and the life your soul knows you were meant for. And social media makes it worse. Now everybody performs happiness like it's a full-time job. People don't even ask, "Am I fulfilled anymore?" They ask, "Do I look fulfilled?"

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: People often ask me when I finally got better, as if there was one magical morning when I opened my eyes and everything felt different. As if healing arrived all at once, like flipping a switch. Darkness one moment, light the next. But that's not how it happened, and honestly, that's not how healing usually works. My depression didn't leave overnight. It left quietly, slowly, almost invisibly, like the tide pulling away from the shore. One day, the water would retreat and I'd catch a glimpse of the beach beneath it. I'd laugh at a video, reply to a message, cook a simple meal, take a walk outside. For a few hours, life felt manageable. Then the tide would return. Not violently, not dramatically, just enough to make me wonder if I'd imagined those better moments. For a long time, that cycle frustrated me. Whenever I felt better, I expected it to stay. Whenever I felt worse, I assumed I was back at the beginning. I didn't realize healing was happening underneath it all. I remember mornings when getting out of bed felt impossible. Not because I was physically tired, because mentally, everything felt heavy. Simple tasks felt enormous: brushing my teeth, taking a shower, answering a text. Things that seemed effortless for everyone else felt like climbing a mountain. And the hardest part was knowing what I was supposed to do. I knew exercise could help, I knew fresh air could help, I knew routines could help. But depression has a way of turning simple actions into impossible missions. Knowing and doing become two completely different things. It's like having a map but no energy to start the journey. Then one day, something happened, something that would seem completely insignificant to most people. I got up and took a shower.

Sign number two: irritability, not sadness. This one catches families completely off guard. When most of us picture depression, we picture someone crying, shutting down, saying they feel hopeless. question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Hi, I'm Chris Avery, I'm the founder of Michaux Media. And this journey for me started back in 2010 while I was deployed to Afghanistan. My mom at the time had sent me a care package, and tucked inside that care package were these stamps featuring this man named Oscar Michaux. Now my mom knew that I had a passion for TV and film, but what she didn't know was that this subtle introduction would drastically change my life. Oscar Michaux lived as a black man during the Great Depression and the segregation of the Jim Crow South. During that time, and despite all of that, he somehow managed to produce, finance, and self-distribute over 40 of his own films entirely independently. He was a maverick who didn't ask for permission. His legacy of self-determination and independence is the absolute inspiration for Michaux Media. Right now, the modern film industry is facing its own unique challenges. Currently, over 85% of the media produced doesn't return its investment, and less than 10% even manages to break even. Hollywood is losing millions because they are bound by outdated production models that fail to engage modern audiences. They are trying to solve a 21st-century problem by gatekeeping 20th-century methods, and it's costing them everything. Michaux Media exists to capture a shift. We want to bet on modern mavericks just like Oscar Michaux. We are building an accelerator platform to de-risk, scale, and monetize creative media before committing massive investment, and shift the power dynamics back to the independent creator. Our platform operates on a four-phase model. First, we host a development sprint designed to test the validity of a project. Second, based on the results of the validation process, we use an internal VC-style model to invest in those ideas that are great and excellent and will go above the mark. And third, we use the most advanced yet financially accessible tools to create proof of concepts. And fourth, we distribute our final result to our pre-vetted and highly curated direct audience. And now is the time for this shift. We are witnessing massive disruption in the entertainment industry. Independent creators are breaking box office records, and we've already seen this in artists like Markiplier and his Iron Lung movie.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: The greatest lie ever told in Silicon Valley is build it and they will come. We love to imagine if you code a brilliant product, users will magically appear, and venture capitalists will throw term sheets at your feet. Investors see countless high-performance products fail because no one ever finds out they exist. Without a distribution plan, a startup is effectively an expensive hobby. Most founders assume investors reject them because their idea is bad. In reality, investors reject them because their pitch deck is completely confusing. Industry veteran Guy Kawasaki points out a classic mistake: cramming slides with 10-point font. If you are reading tiny text aloud to an investor, they read ahead, tune out, and the pitch is dead on arrival. You have to understand the psychology of the person across the table. Venture capitalists see hundreds of pitches a week. They are actively looking for a reason to say no so they can move on to the next one and save time. A pitch deck's utility is limited to surviving that initial wave of skepticism and securing a 30-minute meeting. To survive, you have to clear two psychological hurdles. Hurdle 1: Do I care? To get a yes, your problem statement has to be stupidly simple. If you use MBA jargon to describe a synergistic paradigm, you lose. You need to state exactly how many hours or dollars your user is currently wasting because your product doesn't exist yet. The solution slide should offer immediate relief to that exact pain point. Investors don't want a complex technical schematic of your software architecture here. They want to see the pain disappear. This diagram shows three concentric circles of market size: total addressable market, serviceable available, and serviceable obtainable. This clears Hurdle 2: Is this a real business? Calculate market size here without sounding delusional about capturing all of it day one. That requires detailing your go-to-market strategy. Founders often spend weeks polishing product screenshots and maybe 10 minutes thinking about customer acquisition. A brilliant business model is entirely uninvestable if you can't articulate exactly how your first 100 or 1,000 customers are going to find you. Next is Hurdle 3: Is there proof?

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: The traditional model of higher education is a passive one. You spend years in wood-paneled rooms like this, absorbing information and waiting to be evaluated by a single focal point of authority. But the moment you graduate, that model breaks. You enter a job market that demands prior experience, yet you can't get that experience because no one will hire you without it. It's the universal paradox of the modern graduate. Most students respond by polishing a resume and submitting it to an online portal, hoping to be chosen from a stack of thousands. This path relies entirely on relinquishing control and waiting for someone else to grant you permission to start your career. In an economy that moves as fast as ours, relying on that passive strategy of waiting to be chosen is a losing bet. The traditional line is simply moving too slowly. If you look at how the most significant career opportunities are actually created, they are rarely assigned by a teacher or a hiring manager. They are discovered by people who notice a problem and step in to fix it before they are asked. This suggests a different logical step after graduation. Instead of spending months finding a job, what if you spent a week building a solution to a problem that already exists? There is a sharp contrast in mindset here. A traditional applicant is looking for an empty slot to fill. A creator is looking for a functional gap in the market, and designing a way to close it. Our current economy is full of powerful tools, but short on people who know how to apply them to specific, messy problems. That gap in the market is exactly where students can transition from being consumers of a curriculum to creators of real-world value. Historically, launching a new venture was a high-stakes game. It required massive capital, a team of specialized engineers, and the backing of a large institution. But as this chart shows, the cost of developing a new product has exponentially collapsed, dropping towards zero. Modern artificial intelligence, cloud services, and no-code tools erased those old gates, making infrastructure accessible to anyone with an internet connection. This toolkit has expanded the definition of an entrepreneur. It is no longer a label reserved for business school students. It is now a functional set of skills. For tradespeople scaling a service, artists automating their sales, or educators reaching new students. For example, a student might notice that a local nonprofit struggles with a repetitive administrative bottleneck. Using AI tools, that student can now build a lightweight, functional prototype to solve that specific problem in a single afternoon. Technology has democratized the power to build. This means the primary barrier to entry is no longer capital or a degree. It is the individual decision to hit start. Even with the tools available, most students stay on the sidelines because they feel they lack professional experience. They are waiting for a level of authority that no textbook can give them.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Television framing suggests that a golden key, and investor's approval, is the only way a startup can scale. Yet a growing list of multi-million dollar companies share a counterintuitive origin story. Their trajectory only accelerated after their golden opportunity publicly shattered. Over the last decade, business reality television has engineered a very specific cultural myth: the idea that a panel of billionaires possesses a flawless intuition for predicting market winners. The audience is sold a clean, dramatic narrative. A broadcasted handshake equates to instant wealth and market dominance, while a harsh rejection signifies the immediate death of a company. Behind the cameras, the reality of these negotiations is heavily obscured. Real pitches often last anywhere from 45 minutes to two and a half hours, but editors aggressively splice these marathons down into 8-minute segments designed purely for pacing and conflict. The resulting broadcast is a highly engineered media product. It is optimized for entertainment, capturing dramatic confrontations rather than providing a definitive verdict on a company's fundamental market value. The manipulation of the narrative extends beyond the editing bay. A significant percentage of filmed pitches are completely scrapped by producers, meaning many founders endure the entire gauntlet only to never make it to the airwaves. The psychological toll of the process is severe enough that immediately following a rejection, founders are ushered into a room with a show-appointed psychiatrist to evaluate their mental state before they leave the studio. Even for those who survive the pitch and secure a deal, the instantaneous on-screen handshake is largely theatrical. It is immediately followed by months of grueling off-camera due diligence. During that period of intense scrutiny, the most heavily guarded secret of the production comes to light. Roughly two-thirds of the agreements made on television completely collapse in the real world. Consider the case of HyConn. The founder secured a massive 1.25 million dollar agreement on-air, only to see the entire deal evaporate once the camera stopped rolling and the investor decided to aggressively alter the terms of the agreement. Founders are legally prevented from discussing these collapsed deals or leveraging their television appearance to attract other backers because they are bound by strict non-disclosure agreements enforced by the production company. A televised handshake is a flimsy illusion of success. A startup's true test does not happen in the studio. It begins the exact moment the production crew leaves the room. question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: When you walk into a venture capital pitch, you are stepping into a room defined by heavy skepticism. Every word you say and every slide you show is either building a bridge of trust with the people across the table, or giving them another excuse to say no. The reality of fundraising is that you don't actually win these meetings, you survive them. You keep the conversation alive just long enough to earn a second meeting, by systematically identifying and removing every single reason an investor might hesitate. In 2008, Garrett Camp and Travis Kalanick raised a $200,000 seed round using this presentation. That check grew into an operation valued at $140 billion, even though the deck looks like a rough draft. It runs 25 slides long, ignoring modern advice on brevity. It lacks complex financial models, and barely mentions a business plan. On paper, it should have been discarded during the brutal 3-minute skim test that most VCs use to filter their deal flow. The UberCab deck suggests that at the seed stage, the specific sequencing of trust and psychology can be more influential than the quality of the graphic design. Most founders fall into the trap of the McKinsey-style presentation. They lead with dry market sizing, abstract industry jargon, and theoretical frameworks. It is a logical approach that often feels disconnected from the actual problem being solved. Uber used a structure we call the flipped pyramid. Instead of starting with the math, they hooked the audience with raw, relatable frustration first, saving the spreadsheets for later. They avoided transit industry jargon entirely. Instead, they forced investors to recall the shared misery of trying to hail a cab in a major city. They evoked specific visceral pain points: the 45-minute wait times with zero status updates, and that helpless feeling of standing on a street corner in a downpour hoping an empty car might eventually pass by. Only after they established that emotional wound did they introduce the solution. This direct mapping, linking a technological feature like automated dispatch to a specific human frustration, makes the product feel inevitable. Notice the lack of dense text on these slides. By using simple icons as visual anchors, the deck prevents the investor from reading ahead. It forces the founder to remain the primary storyteller in the room.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: A bill introduced in parliament on Friday could fundamentally change who the Indian state recognizes as transgender and who it doesn't. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill 2026 was tabled in the Lok Sabha by Social Justice Minister Virendra Kumar. And while the government says it's about bringing clarity to a vague law, critics say it could quietly dismantle rights that took years of struggle to win. I'm Vrinda Tulsian and you're watching The Print. To understand what's changed and why it matters, we need to go back to where this all began. It's 2014. The Supreme Court delivers what becomes known as the NALSA judgment, a landmark ruling that recognizes transgender persons as a third gender, directs the government to provide reservations and welfare measures, and crucially holds that a person has the right to self-identify their gender, no surgery required, no medical certificate, no government approval. The court said the constitution guarantees it. That judgment set the stage for legislation, but getting a law passed took five more years, and they weren't smooth years. A 2016 version of the bill was met with protest from the transgender communities across the country. The core objection: it required a District Magistrate to certify whether someone was transgender. Activists said that handed a bureaucrat the power to decide something the Supreme Court had said was a fundamental right. After sustained pressure, the bill was revised. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was finally passed in 2019. It was imperfect, many in the community still had reservations, but it represented a floor, a legal baseline. It defined transgender persons broadly: anyone whose gender doesn't match the gender assigned at birth, including trans men, trans women, genderqueer individuals, those with intersex variations, and those with socio-cultural identities like hijra, kinnar, aravani, and jogta, and it explicitly said, under Section 4, Part 2, that a recognized transgender person has the right to a self-perceived gender identity. answer: Reinventing the wheel doesn't add value or drive change, whether that's to sustainability strategy or to a carbon footprint. So, just on that note, these are the sustainable development goals and these are really broad themes that, I, I find it a really useful exercise with any organization to sit down with the sustainability manager or the health and safety and environment manager or the finance officer, whoever it is who's been tasked with coming up with the sustainability strategy and going through these SDGs and saying, "which really apply to your business, how is your business contributing towards climate action, quality education?" and normally two or three will come out that are incredibly relevant to the business and that can be kind of used as the foundation for how that business should think about sustainability.

answer: On action and duty. Great ideas from the book Meditations by Marcus Aurelius. Just do the right thing, the rest doesn't matter. That quote is basically saying focus on what you can control, and let go of what you can't. Here's what that breaks down to. 1. Just do the right thing. This is the part you can control. It's about your own choices, your own actions, and your own character. Is it kind? Is it honest? Is it helpful? Does it align with who you want to be? Your job is to figure out the right, decent, ethical thing to do in a situation and then do it. That's your duty. 2. The rest doesn't matter. This is the part you can't control, so don't let it paralyze you or stop you from doing your duty. What other people think of you for doing it, whether you'll get credit or even be thanked, whether it will be successful or work out perfectly, how hard or scary it feels. The outcome, sometimes, you can only control your effort, not the final result. Think of it like this. You see someone drop their wallet. The right thing is to pick it up and give it back to them. So you do it. The rest, that doesn't matter. Whether they are suspicious of you, whether they say a heartfelt thank you or just grunt, or whether you're late to your next appointment because you stopped. You did your part. The rest was out of your hands. In a nutshell, pour your energy into being a person of good action. Don't waste your energy worrying about the noise, the results, or the opinions that follow. Your peace comes from knowing you did what you should, not from how the world reacts. It's a call for integrity over image, for courage over comfort, and for focusing on your own behavior in a world you can't control.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: We live our days as if we have an endless supply of tomorrows. But every spring here in Japan, the cherry blossoms remind us of a truth we often try to ignore. A beautiful life isn't one that lasts forever. It is one that blooms fully before the wind takes it away. Every spring, the entire country stops to watch the sakura open. People gather under the trees, lay out blankets, and share food, tea, and be happy together. It's a tradition called Hanami. But if you've never experienced this exact thing in your life, you might not realize what makes the sakura so deeply connected to how we experience life. They only bloom for about 10 to 14 days, sometimes even less. A single strong wind or an early heavy rain can take them all away in one night. And that is exactly why they are so beautiful. If cherry blossoms stayed on the trees forever, nobody would stop to look at them. Since everyone sitting under those trees knows that this moment will not last, they pay attention. They just sit there and soak it in, feeling a deep stillness, aware that the petals are already falling. When I was younger, I used to live as if time was unlimited. I would waste entire days doing things I didn't care about. I would stay in situations that made me unhappy, telling myself I'd change things later. I felt this constant pressure to do everything faster and achieve more, while consistently postponing the things I truly wanted to do. This truth about time really hit me when my grandfather, Daiki, passed away. It happened so quickly that one season, he was sitting with me in his garden, pouring tea and telling me stories. And the next season, his chair was empty, like a petal falling from a branch. After he passed, I was going through his things and found an old journal entry he had written during his last spring. I carry his words with me every single day. He wrote, "Hiroto, the real tragedy of life is how many of our years we waste. The sakura never worries about tomorrow's wind."

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: I got really good at smiling. So good, that nobody noticed the war happening behind my eyes. I laughed loud, showed up, answered messages with "I'm good". Even cracked jokes while my chest felt like it was carrying a thousand pounds of silence. And the scary part is, after a while, even I started believing the performance. See, depression doesn't always look like darkness. Sometimes it looks like being tired all the time for reasons sleep can't fix. Sometimes it looks like staring at the ceiling at 3:00 a.m. replaying every mistake like your mind signed a contract with regret. Sometimes it sounds like, "You're not enough! You're falling behind! Everybody else figured life out except you!" And you begin to drown in thoughts nobody else can hear. That's the thing about invisible pain. People only notice broken bones, not broken spirits. So you learn survival tricks. You become the therapist friend who secretly needs saving. You become the strong one because strong people aren't allowed to collapse. You disappear into music, into work, into scrolling endlessly at night, hoping distraction feels something like peace. But silence, silence is dangerous. Because when you sit alone long enough, you meet every version of yourself you tried to outrun. The insecure child, the abandoned heart, the exhausted soul. And one day, I realized I wasn't just fighting depression. I was fighting the version of me that believed I had to earn love by suffering quietly. I thought healing meant never hurting again. But healing is actually waking up and choosing to stay, even when your mind tells you to disappear. Healing is messy. It's crying in parked cars, it's canceling plans to breathe, it's admitting, "I'm not okay." before your breaking point introduces you to the ground.

answer: Our poster presentation documents the creation of a rubric by a group of librarians at American University to evaluate which AI tools, if any, made sense for us to subscribe to and promote. We ended up creating this rubric ourselves because we couldn't find an already extant tool that fit our needs, and we thought detailing our process might be helpful to other institutions currently considering the adoption of AI tools. Our university librarian asked our department to pilot an AI research tool. This group then decided to review AI tools focused on the literature review process. Literature review tools were selected for a few reasons. One, they're discipline agnostic. We're a social science heavy institution, which tends to be pretty interdisciplinary. Two, faculty, students, and staff all do literature reviews. And three, there are a number of AI tools with literature reviews built specifically in mind. In order to determine how we would evaluate these tools, we met as a group and discussed what we would want a rubric to measure. We reviewed some of the literature related to this, there wasn't much, and determined the questions by consensus. We then created a survey in Qualtrics. We divided up the list evenly between group members, with some claiming tools in which they were particularly interested or had experience with. Then, each member analyzed three to four tools and recorded the results in Qualtrics. Ithaka, the nonprofit behind JSTOR, has created the Ithaka Generative AI Product Tracker that lists generative AI tools that can be used for postsecondary teaching, learning, or research activities. The tracker includes roughly 150 AI tools and counting, many of which support key stages of the research lifecycle, including discovery, understanding, and creation. answer: Imagine I asked you, what do you learn in law school? Well, you've decided to take this course, so maybe you're more informed than the average person. So instead imagine I asked your college roommate or your parents, assuming they're not lawyers. The image that may come to mind of law school is sun-deprived, bespectacled law students surrounded by large numbers of dusty books, reading intently so they can memorize a bunch of law cases. And don't get me wrong, we do make students read a lot from books, and there's some memorization involved. But that image of someone learning the law by just memorizing things that are already out there is not at all what law school is really about. If it were, law school would be much less fun, and also much less useful. The law is always changing. So if you just learned a number of dry rules, much of what you learned might be outdated by your fifth year in practice. The chief value of legal education is not to know stuff, but to know what stuff to look for, where to find it, how to interpret what you find, what to think when some stuff says one thing, and other stuff says another. And how to use what you find to give legal advice. Let me put this very tangibly for you. If you call up a lawyer on anything other than a very simple question, and without pausing, she quickly gives you a straightforward answer, you should fire her. She's not doing a very good job for you. She's just not thinking like a lawyer. That's a phrase you'll hear a lot in law school, and while we might over-use it a bit, it does capture something important. Law is mostly about questions, choices, and analysis, about thinking and not so much about simple answers. That is the main thing we try to teach you in law school. Yes, we want to teach you a good amount of content about the law. To use an example from a course I teach, civil procedure, we want you to know what claims without subject matter jurisdiction can get jurisdiction by way of being joined to other claims through 28 U.S.C. 1367. If that sounds a bit intimidating at first, that's very normal, it is. But by the end of 1L fall, that knowledge will be at the tip of your brain, or at least somewhere in there.

And though the cops still won't verify their authenticity, because of something that I'm going to get into in just a little bit, it is important to read them in full. So here we go. The first alleged note that was apparently sent on February 2nd says this, "Hello, Savannah. We have your mother, Nancy. She is safe but scared. She will be held for ransom and once payment is received, she will be released unharmed. We will be holding her for a maximum of 7 days. You will need to send Bitcoin in the amount of $4 million USD, United States Dollars, before 5:00 p.m. on Thursday the 5th. If payment is not received, the ransom will be increased to $6 million USD, which will need to be paid by 5:00 p.m. on Monday the 9th. Once payment is received to the Bitcoin address below, she will be released within 12 hours of deposit to a safe drop-off location back in Tucson. If payment is not received by the last deadline on Monday the 9th at 5:00 p.m., she will be killed. Your mother is aware of this, and her life is in your hands. It is in the best interest of everyone to have this completed as soon as possible. You will not be able to contact me from here on out. There will be no negotiation. Do not play games. Law enforcement will not be able to help you. She had a white smartwatch on the floor of the foot of her bed, and the white floodlight in back yard was destroyed."

Then you have the second alleged note. Very different, very different tone. This was apparently sent on February 6th, so 3 days before the deadline from that first note. It says, "Guthrie family, we did not fully grasp the seriousness of her physical condition. We never intended to hurt her, that was not our intention. She perished shortly after she was taken. We believe it was heart-related. She is buried in nature now. Nothing you could have done could have changed the outcome. We want your family to know this, and hope you can find peace. We are truly sorry."
